source_text: Cum ergo bene definita sit voluntas: Motus animi, cogente nullo, quid quaeris superius causas, quas definitio voluntatis exclusit? Expendite igitur quid sit voluntas, et desinetis inquirere unde sit voluntas. Voluntas est enim motus animi, cogente nullo; vos, si tentetis ire dimidio ungue superius, statim constituta convellitis. Quid ergo dicit Manichaeus? Sed iste motus ideo exortus est, quia de tenebrarum natura homo factus est. Quid tu? Quia, inquis, de nihilo factus est homo. Unus ergo dicit: Ideo voluntas mala, quia de nihilo factus est homo; alter: Ideo voluntas mala in homine, quia de tenebris factus est homo. Utrique ergo illud voluntatis suppletorium denegatis, id est, cogente nullo. Si enim tanta fuit virtus in nihilo, quanta in aliquo; quae coegit hanc voluntatem existere, exclusit ab ea conditionem suam, qua dictum fuerat, cogente nullo. Sed non minus mali abegit infamiam; non est enim peccatum, quod de motu animi libero non venit; effectumque est ut cum dispendio veritatis, totius mali periret invidia; et evanuit mali natura, cum crimen voluntatis evanuit; crimen autem evanuit voluntatis, cum definitio voluntatis exsecta est. Et peccati igitur et voluntatis claruit eiusmodi esse conditionem, ut si causis praecedentibus deputetur, et ius eo perdat, et crimen. Ubi ergo erit mali natura, cum malum non esse constiterit?
pass_a_gloss: When therefore will has been well defined: A motion of the mind, no one compelling, why do you ask higher causes which the definition of will excluded? Weigh therefore what will is, and you will cease to inquire from where will is. For will is a motion of the mind, no one compelling; you, if you try to go a half fingernail higher, immediately tear the constitutions. What therefore does Manichaeus say? But this motion therefore arose, because the human was made from the nature of darkness. What you? Because, you say, the human was made from nothing. One therefore says: Therefore an evil will, because the human was made from nothing; the other: Therefore an evil will in the human, because the human was made from darkness. Both therefore deny that supplement of will, that is, no one compelling. For if there was as great a virtue in nothing as in something; which compelled this will to exist, it excluded from it its own condition, by which it had been said, no one compelling. But it did not less drive off the infamy of evil; for it is not sin, which does not come from a free motion of the mind; and it was effected that with a loss of truth the spite of the whole evil would perish; and the nature of evil vanished, when the charge of will vanished; but the charge of will vanished, when the definition of will was cut out. And of sin therefore and of will it has become clear that the condition is of such a kind, that if it is assigned to preceding causes, it loses both right by that, and the charge. Where therefore will the nature of evil be, when it has stood that there is not evil?

LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself

pass_b_english: Since will is well defined as ‘a movement of the mind under no compulsion,’ why do you seek earlier causes which the definition of will has excluded? Weigh what will is, and you will stop asking where will comes from. Will is a movement of the mind under no compulsion. If you try to go so much as half a fingernail beyond this, you immediately overthrow what has been established. What does Mani say? ‘This movement arose because the human being was made from the nature of darkness.’ What do you say? ‘Because the human being was made from nothing.’ Thus one says, ‘The will is evil because the human being was made from nothing’; the other, ‘The will is evil in a human being because he was made from darkness.’ Both of you deny what completes the will’s definition: ‘under no compulsion.’ If nothing had as much power as something, and that power compelled this will to exist, it excluded the will’s own condition, expressed as ‘under no compulsion.’

But it has equally driven away evil’s disgrace. What does not come from a free movement of the mind is not sin. Thus, at the expense of truth, all the odium of evil perished. Evil’s nature vanished when the will’s guilt vanished; the will’s guilt vanished when the definition of will was cut apart. It has therefore become clear that the condition of both sin and will is such that, if attributed to preceding causes, it loses both its freedom and its guilt. Where, then, will evil’s nature be, once it is established that no evil exists?

choices.why: Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.
Julian's standing charge: natural evil is Manichaean. Keep the sect-name, not 'dualists'.
